traveler: Johannes Trithemius (Johann von Heidenberg), abbot of Sponheim and of St James's at Würzburg
title: The Snowstorm at Sponheim: the Abbot, the Two Thousand Volumes, and the Book That Was Not Magic
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Moselle and the Stepfather's House

stops.name: Trittenheim, birth on the Moselle
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: In the village of Trittenheim on the Moselle, in the Electorate of Trier, a son is born to Johann von Heidenberg and his wife Elisabeth on the first of February. They christen him Johann. The father dies while the child is still an infant. The parish church of the village is St. Clemens and the slopes above the river are vineyards. No document names the house. The boy will take his surname from this place, in the humanist fashion of the century, and five hundred years after his birth the village will raise a statue to the name it gave him.
suggested_refs: The parish church of St. Clemens at Trittenheim, the village that gave him his name

stops.name: Trittenheim, the stepfather and the three languages
stops.date_confidence: computed: English Wikipedia dates the remarriage seven years after the father's death in 1462; the years of secret study are given only as boyhood, undated
stops.campa: Seven years after her husband's death Elisabeth remarries. The stepfather has no use for books and forbids the boy his studies; the English and German accounts agree on that hostility and record nothing else whatever about the man. Johann works in secret and without a master, and by the time he leaves the house he reads Greek, Latin, and Hebrew. The only source for this is Trithemius himself, writing much later, and he names neither a schoolmaster nor a single book he learned from.
suggested_refs: Trithemius's own autobiographical passages, the sole authority for the years of concealed study

stops.name: Trier, the first stop of the flight
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the sources give his age as about seventeen and name no month
stops.campa: At about seventeen he leaves the Moselle village and does not come back to live in it. The road runs first to Trier, the old imperial city downstream, seat of the Elector in whose territory he was born, where the cathedral of St. Peter has stood on Roman foundations for eleven centuries. The German account gives the escape as a bare list of place names: Trier, Cologne, the Netherlands, Heidelberg. It names no companion and no patron, and gives no month. Nothing survives of what the boy carried or how he paid his way.
suggested_refs: The Hohe Domkirche St. Peter at Trier, landmark of the electoral capital he passed through

stops.name: Cologne, the second stop, seven years before the pupil
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the route is attested, its internal sequence dated only as c. 1479
stops.campa: The road runs downriver to Cologne, where the cathedral has stood half-built for two centuries with a crane rusting on the stump of its south tower. The city means nothing yet to the boy passing through it. Seven years after he walks these streets Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa will be born here, and twenty-three years after that Agrippa will ride to Würzburg to sit with him for several days over the question of what natural magic is, and will dedicate the draft of his own book to him the following spring.
sources: QUEUE.md line 151 and census_real_persons_2026-08-02.md line 505, both glossing him as 'teacher of Agrippa'
suggested_refs: Cologne, birthplace of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa in 1486, queued for the atlas and not yet researched

stops.name: The Netherlands, a country with no town in it
stops.date_confidence: unresolved: the route is attested for c. 1479, the position within it is a guess
stops.campa: The route carries him on into the Netherlands and then turns him back toward the Rhine. That is the whole of the record. No town is named, no school, no length of stay, no reason for going and no reason for returning. The pin sits at the geographic centre of the country because the sources give a country and nothing smaller; it marks a gap rather than a place where anyone can say he stood. Of the four stages of the flight this is the one rubbed out entirely. The next name on the list is Heidelberg.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Johannes Trithemius' (route given as Trier, Köln, Niederlande, Heidelberg)
suggested_refs: An unresolved waypoint: no source names a Netherlandish town in the flight of c. 1479

stops.name: Heidelberg, the only university he will attend
stops.date_confidence: traditional: arrival c. 1479 and study to 1482, with no matriculation date in the reachable sources
stops.campa: He reaches Heidelberg and studies there about three years, the only formal university education of his life. The buildings shown to visitors as the old university went up between 1712 and 1728 and have nothing to do with him. In 1487 a magister named Georgius Helmstetter will take his degree in this town, and later scholars will identify that man with Faust; in April 1518 Martin Luther will defend his theses here before the Augustinians. Trithemius will have been sixteen months in the ground by then.
suggested_refs: The medieval University of Heidelberg, founded 1386; the Alte Universität building is a later structure and is not his

stops.name: Sponheim Abbey, the snowstorm and the novice
stops.date_confidence: attested as event; the month is traditional, and the whole anecdote descends from Trithemius's own account
stops.campa: Travelling home from Heidelberg he is caught in a snowstorm in the hills above the Nahe and asks shelter at the Benedictine house of Sponheim, near Bad Kreuznach. He does not leave. Within days he asks to be received as a novice, and takes in religion the name of the village he was born in. The abbey he has walked into is poor, ill-disciplined, and holds about forty-eight books. He is twenty years old and has, so far, no library of his own and no plan that anybody wrote down.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Sponheim Abbey; the former abbey church now serves as the parish church of St. Maria and St. Martin

stops.name: Sponheim, elected abbot at twenty-one
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day by German Wikipedia; a source giving his age as twenty-five is arithmetically wrong and is not followed
stops.campa: Eighteen months after the snowstorm the monks elect the novice their abbot. He is twenty-one, born in February 1462 and raised over the house in July 1483, and he inherits a monastery in material and spiritual disrepair. He will hold it for twenty-two years, ruling a house whose discipline he never repairs while he builds the largest private library in Germany. The books he writes in those same years will earn a reputation that makes the community ungovernable for him.
suggested_refs: The abbatial succession lists of Sponheim, where he enters as the twenty-one-year-old elected in July 1483

stops.name: Sponheim, the abbatial blessing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; whether the ceremony took place at Sponheim or elsewhere is not stated in any source
stops.campa: On the ninth of November Berthold von Oberg, suffragan bishop of Mainz, gives the young abbot the abbatial blessing and confirms him in office. The German account records the date and the bishop's name and not the church. From this day Trithemius is a prelate entitled to mitre and crosier, at an age when the men he sat beside at Heidelberg are still students. He begins by buying books, and by writing to every religious house, bookseller, and printer within reach of the Nahe who might be persuaded to part with one.
suggested_refs: Berthold von Oberg, suffragan bishop of Mainz, who blessed him in office on 9 November 1483

stops.name: Sponheim, the library
stops.date_confidence: period: the library grows across the whole abbacy, 1483 to 1505, and is fixed here at a single year for the map
stops.campa: The forty-eight volumes become hundreds and then more than two thousand, printed and manuscript, Greek and Hebrew as well as Latin, the largest private collection in Germany. Scholars cross the Empire to see it, and the abbot of a small house on the Nahe becomes a correspondent of humanists, bishops, and in time an emperor. He buys, borrows, copies, and commissions. The library is the instrument of everything he writes, and its cost is one of the grievances that will finally turn his own monks against him.
suggested_refs: The Sponheim library, dispersed after 1556 and absorbed into the Bibliotheca Palatina at Heidelberg in 1601

stops.name: Sponheim, the catalogues of other men's books
stops.date_confidence: 1491 for the Catalogus and 1494 for De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, both by year only, per 1911 Britannica
stops.campa: He compiles the Catalogus illustrium virorum Germaniae, a register of eminent Germans, and three years later De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, a survey of the writers of the Church. These are the works later scholarship judges the most trustworthy of anything he produced. Elsewhere he invents chroniclers, gives them names, Hunibald and Meginfrid, and quotes and defends them in print. The bibliographies hold up. The histories will take three centuries to sort out.
suggested_refs: De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis, 1494, one of the founding works of European literary bibliography

stops.name: Bursfelde, the congregation that met elsewhere
stops.date_confidence: the role is attested for 1492-1503; the pin is the congregation's mother house, not a meeting place he is known to have visited
stops.campa: For eleven years he is featured speaker and chapter secretary at the annual general chapters of the Bursfelde Congregation, the reformed Benedictine union of northern Germany, and he is one of its loudest voices for monastic discipline. The pin here is a caution rather than an address. Of sixty-eight general chapters held between 1458 and 1530, only eleven convened at Bursfelde itself, the congregation preferring more central houses. Which towns he actually rode to in those eleven years is recorded nowhere reachable.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Kloster Bursfelde' (eleven of sixty-eight chapters held at the mother house, 1458-1530)
suggested_refs: The acts of the Bursfelde general chapters, 1492-1503, whose meeting places for those years are an open gap

stops.name: Sponheim, in praise of the copying hand
stops.date_confidence: written 1492 per the English Wikipedia works list, which reads '1492 (printed 1494)'
stops.campa: He writes De laude scriptorum manualium, in praise of the scribes: a monk who copies a book by hand does work that a machine cannot do, and parchment written by hand outlasts paper struck by type. His own library is full of printed books and he buys them faster than anyone in the Rhineland. The argument is about discipline rather than about the press: copying is a practice, and a house that gives it up loses something it will not notice losing until it is gone.
suggested_refs: De laude scriptorum manualium, the monastic defence of the scribe written on the eve of the print century

stops.name: Mainz, the treatise goes to the press
stops.date_confidence: attested: printed 1494 at Mainz by Peter von Friedberg, per the English Wikipedia works list
stops.campa: Two years after he writes it, the praise of hand-copying is set in movable type by Peter von Friedberg at Mainz, in the city where Gutenberg cut the first European type a lifetime earlier. Trithemius sends it to the press himself. He wants the argument read, and the fastest way to be read in 1494 is the machine the argument is about. It is among the earliest defences of the scribe to reach a press, and the joke that has been made at its expense has lasted as long as the book has.
suggested_refs: The Mainz press of Peter von Friedberg, printer of the 1494 De laude scriptorum manualium

stops.name: Sponheim, the two chronicles
stops.date_confidence: Chronicon Sponheimense c. 1495-1509 and Chronicon Hirsaugiense 1495-1503; the two-volume Annales Hirsaugienses is a separate and later work of 1509-1514
stops.campa: He begins the Chronicon Sponheimense, a history of his own abbey and the counts who founded it, and alongside it the Chronicon Hirsaugiense, a history of the Benedictine house at Hirsau. The Sponheim chronicle will still be growing in 1509, four years after he has left the building. These two carry his invented authorities, the chroniclers he names and quotes and defends, and the nineteenth century will spend decades deciding which of their charters and abbots ever existed.
sources: 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Trithemius, Johannes' (which lists only the Annales hirsaugienses)
suggested_refs: The Annales Hirsaugienses, 1509-1514, published at St. Gallen in 1690, the two-volume expansion of the Hirsau chronicle

stops.name: Sponheim, the book of hidden writing
stops.date_confidence: composed 1499-1500; the printed text heads the work 1500
stops.campa: Inside the abbey he writes Steganographia, three books that read as a manual for sending messages by angels and are in fact a manual for sending messages in cipher. He dedicates it to Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine, and signs himself Abbas Spanheimensis. He does not print it. It circulates in manuscript among correspondents he trusts, and the preface says plainly why: the secret is to be wrapped in mysteries so that nobody untrained can reach it. The wrapping will be believed for four hundred years.
stops.quote: Ne autem hoc magnum secretum in aures vulgarium imperitorum aut prauorum hominum perueniat, officij mei rationem existimaui non vltimam, ita illud, quoniam mysteria docet intelligere nescientem, mysterijs obuoluere
stops.quote_source: Steganographia, dedicatory epistle to Philip, Count Palatine of the Rhine; Latin transcription by Joseph H. Peterson, esotericarchives.com/tritheim/stegano.htm (the page carries no English)
sources: Joseph H. Peterson's Latin transcription at esotericarchives.com/tritheim/stegano.htm
suggested_refs: The manuscript circulation of Steganographia, 1500-1606, from which every rumour about its author grew

stops.name: Bad Kreuznach, the library carried out of the war
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year by German Wikipedia, 'Kloster Sponheim'; no month is given
stops.campa: The Landshut War of Succession reaches the Nahe country, and the abbot loads the library, the treasury, and the abbey archives onto carts and moves the lot into the town of Kreuznach for safekeeping. Twenty years of buying travels a few miles under guard. Three years from now he will write a letter naming a wandering boaster who has just been given the schoolmaster's post in this same town through the patronage of the knight Franz von Sickingen, and who fled it under an accusation of sodomy. That man is the first Faust on record.
sources: johann_faust.journey.json (stop 'Bad Kreuznach, the schoolmaster who fled')
suggested_refs: The Ebernburg above the Nahe, seat of Franz von Sickingen, pinned in johann_faust.journey.json as an explicit reconstruction

stops.name: Sponheim, the resignation
stops.date_confidence: contradiction left open: German Wikipedia gives 1505, the English article on Sponheim Abbey gives 1506; the stop takes the earlier of the two
stops.campa: He gives up the abbacy after twenty-two years. The monks have resisted his discipline and resented the cost and the custody of the library, and the whisper about the book of angel-writing has reached the people whose favour he needs. Nobody tries him and nobody condemns him. He becomes, inside his own house, a man whose reputation is a liability. He leaves the two thousand volumes behind him; over the next three centuries they will travel to Heidelberg and then to Rome, and the abbey will be pulled down.
suggested_refs: The Sponheim abbatial records for 1505-1506, whose disagreement over the year of resignation is not resolved

segments.name: Würzburg, the Abbey of the Scots

stops.name: Boppard, the emperor's eight questions
stops.date_confidence: traditional: writing in 1508, Trithemius recalls the Boppard meeting as dudum, some time ago; 1505 is the conventional dating and no source fixes a day
stops.campa: In the castle at Boppard on the Rhine, Maximilian I puts eight questions to the abbot: on witches, on the nature of God, on the origin of evil spirits, on the sins that damn. Trithemius answers them at the table and, three years later, in writing, opening the book by reciting the emperor's own commission. He is now a man that emperors send for. He is also a man about to lose his abbey, and the two facts arrive within months of each other. The Rhine castle is where the questions are asked; the answers will be written far to the east.
stops.quote: PARVI MANDATIS tuis Maximiliane Cesar inuictissime: & eas questiones octo quas mihi dudum ad celsitudinem tuam vocato in Castello Bopardiano proposuisti
stops.quote_source: Liber octo quaestionum, opening address to Maximilian I; Latin transcription by Joseph H. Peterson, esotericarchives.com/tritheim/8quest.htm (Latin only, no English on the page)
sources: Joseph H. Peterson's Latin transcription at esotericarchives.com/tritheim/8quest.htm
suggested_refs: The imperial castle at Boppard, where Maximilian I put the eight questions to the abbot of Sponheim

stops.name: Würzburg, abbot of the Schottenkloster
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Lorenz von Bibra, prince-bishop of Würzburg, offers him the abbacy of St James's, the Schottenkloster, the house of the Scots and Irish on the left bank of the Main. He takes it and holds it until he dies. The house is smaller than Sponheim and its library is nothing, but the bishop is a patron rather than an opponent, and the town is a bishop's capital with a court in it. Everything he writes from here on is written in this building, which the war of 1945 will burn and which is now a church of the Salesians.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Johannes Trithemius' (Schottenanger 15, today the Don-Bosco-Kirche)
suggested_refs: The Schottenkloster St. Jakob in the Mainviertel, Schottenanger 15, rebuilt after 1945 as the Don-Bosco-Kirche

stops.name: Innsbruck, the emperor's summons and the shade of Mary of Burgundy
stops.date_confidence: the two summonses are attested for 1506-1507 with no place named; the necromancy story is undated legend, and Innsbruck stands in for Maximilian's usual residence
stops.campa: Twice in these two years he is summoned to Maximilian's court, and no source says where the court was standing when he arrived. The pin is Innsbruck because Innsbruck is where the emperor mostly was. Long after both men are dead, Luther's table talk and a Protestant pamphlet of 1585 will tell a different story about these audiences: that the abbot raised Alexander the Great and the emperor's dead wife Mary of Burgundy for him, and that the apparition wore a birthmark on the neck which only the widower knew about.
stops.quote: a magician and necromancer (understood to be Trithemius) who summoned Alexander the Great and other ancient heroes, as well as the emperor's deceased wife Mary of Burgundy, to entertain Maximilian
stops.quote_source: English Wikipedia, 'Johannes Trithemius', summarising Martin Luther's Tischreden (1569 edition) and Augustin Lercheimer's account of 1585
suggested_refs: The Hofburg at Innsbruck, placeholder for an imperial audience whose location no source records

stops.name: Würzburg, the letter to Virdung
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the original letter is in the Vatican Library
stops.campa: He writes to the astrologer Johannes Virdung of Hassfurt about a boaster he has run into at Gelnhausen, a man who styles himself with a chain of titles and claims he could reproduce the miracles of Christ. Trithemius calls him a charlatan and a fool and warns Virdung not to receive him. It is the earliest surviving description of the man the world will call Faust, written by a Benedictine abbot to save an astrologer an afternoon, and the whole legend of the pact and the damnation grows from it.
stops.quote: Magister Georgius Sabellicus, Faustus iunior. fons necromanticorum, astrologus, magus secundus, chiromanticus, agromanticus, pyromanticus, in hydra arte secundus.
stops.quote_source: Trithemius to Johannes Virdung, 20 August 1507, reporting how the man styled himself; Latin per German Wikipedia, 'Johann Georg Faust' (English Wikipedia truncates the string at magus secundus, and 'aeromanticus' is a common editorial emendation of 'agromanticus')
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Johann Georg Faust' (full Latin string, original in the Vatican Library)
English Wikipedia, 'Johann Georg Faust' (truncated string, 20 August 1507)
suggested_refs: The Trithemius letter to Virdung of 20 August 1507, Vatican Library, the first documentary Faust

stops.name: Würzburg, the eight questions answered
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; four works are dated 1508 and the sources give no order among them
stops.campa: He writes out the Liber octo quaestionum for Maximilian. On God he quotes the figure of the sphere whose centre is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere, ascribing it to Empedocles as his century did, and invokes Nicholas of Cusa, his countryman from the Moselle, a few lines later. On witches he quotes Exodus, Maleficos non patieris viuere, and argues that they are to be tolerated nowhere and rooted out of every place entirely. The same book holds both sentences.
stops.quote: Propterea pulchre similitudinem dedit empedocles dicens. Deus est sphera cuius centrum vbique: circumferentia nusquam.
stops.quote_source: Liber octo quaestionum; Latin transcription by Joseph H. Peterson, esotericarchives.com/tritheim/8quest.htm (the formula in fact descends from the pseudo-Hermetic Liber XXIV philosophorum, transmitted through Alain de Lille and Cusanus)
sources: Joseph H. Peterson's Latin transcription at esotericarchives.com/tritheim/8quest.htm
suggested_refs: Nicholas of Cusa, the other Moselle theologian, whom Trithemius cites by name in the same passage

stops.name: Würzburg, against the sorcerers
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the dedication to Joachim I, Elector of Brandenburg, comes from general reference knowledge and was not re-verified against a live source
stops.campa: He writes the Antipalus maleficiorum, a treatise against witchcraft, and catalogues in its first book the grimoires he wants suppressed, describing each one closely enough that it can be recognised and burned. Of one he writes that it teaches men to pray to spirits and sacrifice to the planets. The man denouncing these books is the man who wrote Steganographia nine years earlier, and he keeps no distance between the two positions: his cipher-book is lawful because it is not what it appears to be, and the grimoires are damnable because they are.
stops.quote: Spiritibus orationes facit, & offert sacrificium planetis.
stops.quote_source: Antipalus maleficiorum, Book I, catalogue entry 81, Trithemius describing a condemned grimoire rather than quoting one; Latin at esotericarchives.com/tritheim/antipalus.htm
suggested_refs: The catalogue of condemned grimoires in Antipalus maleficiorum, Book I, an inventory of magic books that survives only because a censor wrote it

stops.name: Würzburg, the seven planetary angels
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; first printed at Nuremberg in 1522 by Johann Haselberg, printer Hieronymus Höltzel
stops.campa: He writes De septem secundeis for Maximilian: a history of the world divided into cycles of three hundred and fifty-four years and four months, each governed by one of seven planetary angels, running from the Creation to a date well past his own death. It is astrological world-history of the kind the emperor collects. At the very end, having laid out the entire scheme, he attaches a protestation of orthodoxy in his own hand, and the seven angels are handed back to the Church in a single sentence.
stops.quote: I protest with my own proper hand, and confess with my own mouth, that in all these things delivered, I beleeve nothing, or admit of anything, unless what the Catholick Church doth hold: the rest, I refute and contemn as vain, faigned and superstitious.
stops.quote_source: De septem secundeis, closing protestation, in William Lilly's English of 1647 printed in The Worlds Catastrophe; the Latin stands beside it at esotericarchives.com/tritheim/tritem.htm
suggested_refs: William Lilly's 1647 translation of De septem secundeis, printed in The Worlds Catastrophe

stops.name: Würzburg, Polygraphia
stops.date_confidence: written 1508 per English Wikipedia; German Wikipedia instead describes composition spanning 1508-1515 in six volumes, and the disagreement is left open
stops.campa: He finishes Polygraphia, six books of substitution alphabets and tables, among them the square grid of shifted alphabets later called the tabula recta, which will still be taught as the foundation of polyalphabetic cipher four centuries later. He does not print this one either. It appears in 1518, two years after he is buried, and it is the first book on cryptography ever published. The abbot who argued that scribes should copy by hand has now written the manual for making a hand-copied text unreadable.
suggested_refs: The tabula recta of Polygraphia, Book V, ancestor of every polyalphabetic cipher down to the Vigenere square

stops.name: Einsiedeln, the tutors who were never there
stops.date_confidence: undated legend, given a placeholder year in the boyhood of Paracelsus; no source places Trithemius at Einsiedeln at any date
stops.campa: Later biographers of Paracelsus put the boy's schooling at the Benedictine abbey of Einsiedeln in Schwyz, under four bishops and under Trithemius. No record puts Trithemius in Switzerland, at Einsiedeln or anywhere else, for any length of time, and none puts Paracelsus at Sponheim or Würzburg before the abbot's death. The pin marks a claim, not a journey. What probably happened is the ordinary thing: Paracelsus read him, the ideas travelled in books, and the tradition afterwards supplied a room and a teacher to carry them.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Paracelsus' (flagging the Einsiedeln tutors as unsubstantiated tradition)
suggested_refs: Einsiedeln Abbey in Schwyz, birthplace of Paracelsus and site of a tutelage no document supports

stops.name: Würzburg, the abbot and the secret art
stops.date_confidence: traditional: the atlas already carries this pin from paracelsus.journey.json; direct documentary evidence of the meeting is thin and the claim rests on later tradition and on Paracelsus's own admiring references
stops.campa: Theophrastus von Hohenheim, not yet calling himself Paracelsus, is said to come to Würzburg and learn alchemy and the hidden sciences from the abbot of the Schottenkloster. It rests on tradition, not on a document. A rival claimant exists besides, Salomon Trismosin, also called his teacher. Both traditions stand, and neither is settled here.
sources: paracelsus.journey.json (stop 'Wurzburg, the abbot Trithemius and the secret art', 1508-04-01)
johann_faust.journey.json (noting Trithemius will teach alchemy in this city within the year)
QUEUE.md line 152 (Salomon Trismosin, rival teacher tradition)
suggested_refs: paracelsus.journey.json, the pin inherited byte-identically from the pupil's own file

stops.name: Würzburg, the winter with Agrippa
stops.date_confidence: attested to the winter of 1509-1510 by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; no exact date is given
stops.campa: Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, twenty-three years old, comes to St James's Abbey from Dole, where his lectures have already drawn a heresy denunciation from the Franciscan prior Jean Catilinet and from which he will be forced out the following year. He and the abbot talk for several days about natural magic. Agrippa was born in Cologne in 1486, seven years after a runaway from the Moselle passed through that city on his way to find a school he could get into.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim'
English Wikipedia, 'Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa' (forced to leave Dole in 1510, after the visit)
suggested_refs: The several days of conversation on natural magic at Würzburg, winter 1509-1510, source of the first De occulta philosophia

stops.name: Würzburg, the letter of the eighth of April
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: Shortly before the eighth of April, Agrippa sends him the first draft of De occulta philosophia and dedicates it to him. Trithemius writes back praising the book, telling the young man to ground his magic in deeper philosophy and metaphysics, and advising him to keep his occult studies to himself, which is the counsel of a man who did not keep his own quiet enough. Ten years on, four years after the abbot is dead, the corpus of Trithemius's magical manuscripts passes into Agrippa's hands and goes into the final version of that book.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim' (the 1510 dedication and the 1520 acquisition of the manuscripts)
suggested_refs: The 1510 manuscript draft of De occulta philosophia, dedicated to Trithemius and revised for twenty years afterwards

stops.name: Würzburg, death at St James's
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He dies in the Schottenkloster on the thirteenth of December, fifty-four years old, ten years abbot of the house, and is buried in its church. Polygraphia is unprinted. Steganographia is unprinted and will stay in manuscript another ninety years. De septem secundeis will wait six years for a press at Nuremberg. Nothing that made his later reputation, in either direction, is in circulation on the day of the funeral. What the mourners know of him is a chronicler, a bibliographer, and a reformer of Benedictine houses.
suggested_refs: The abbey church of St. Jakob at Würzburg, his burial place, destroyed in 1945 and rebuilt

stops.name: Würzburg, Riemenschneider cuts the slab
stops.date_confidence: c. 1516, workshop attribution; the relief carries no date in the sources consulted
stops.campa: Tilman Riemenschneider, or the workshop he runs in this town, carves the memorial relief: the abbot in pontifical vestments, with mitre and crosier. The relief carries no date in the sources and the attribution runs to the workshop rather than the hand. It is the likeness that every later portrait of Trithemius descends from, and the only piece of him that will still be above ground four hundred years on. No source records what the epitaph cost or who paid for it. The grave will stay where it was dug. The slab will not.
suggested_refs: The Riemenschneider tomb relief of Trithemius, source of the standard iconography of the abbot

stops.name: Würzburg, the Neumünster
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the transfer of the slab; the restoration after 1945 is undated in the sources
stops.campa: In 1825 the tombstone is lifted out of the old Schottenkloster and set up in the Neumünster, the collegiate church beside the cathedral, a foundation going back to about 1057 under Bishop Adalbero and rebuilt in baroque between 1711 and 1716. The relief moves; the body does not, and no source says the remains were ever translated. In 1945 the bombing of Würzburg damages the slab, and the workshop of Theodor Spiegel puts it back together. It is still there, less than a kilometre from the grave.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Johannes Trithemius' ('In 1825, the tombstone was relocated to the Neumünster church')
suggested_refs: The Neumünster collegiate church at Würzburg, where the epitaph has stood since 1825

stops.name: Oppenheim, Polygraphia goes to press
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the place of printing is unresolved, with Oppenheim, Mainz, and Reichenau all appearing in the reachable sources and no printer confirmed
stops.campa: Two years after the funeral the six books of Polygraphia are printed, the first book on cryptography ever published, and the tabula recta enters the public record. Where exactly it was printed is a mess the sources do not clear up: Oppenheim, Mainz, and Reichenau all appear, and no one names the printer. The pin takes one of the three and the disagreement stands. The content travels regardless, because a cipher table can be copied by any reader who owns the book once.
suggested_refs: The 1518 editio princeps of Polygraphia, whose imprint city is not settled in the reachable sources

stops.name: Cologne, the manuscripts change hands
stops.date_confidence: the year 1520 is attested exactly by the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; no source names a place, and the pin is Agrippa's birth city rather than an attested site of transfer
stops.campa: The corpus of magical manuscripts that had belonged to Trithemius comes into Agrippa's possession. The Stanford encyclopedia gives the year and not the place; the pin is the city Agrippa was born in, which is a guess and is marked as one. He works the material into the revised De occulta philosophia, the book that becomes the standard handbook of Renaissance magic, including for the men who assemble Faust. What the abbot told him to keep secret is now setting in type.
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Agrippa von Nettesheim' ('came into Agrippa's possession in 1520')
suggested_refs: The three-book De occulta philosophia of 1533, carrying material from Trithemius's own manuscripts

stops.name: Prague, the descent of the angel alphabet
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no document links Trithemius to Rudolf II's Prague, and the pin marks a tradition the corpus already carries rather than an event
stops.campa: At the court of Rudolf II, John Dee and Edward Kelley run their scrying sessions and record an angelic alphabet and a language dictated by spirits. That much is documented, unlike the Faust house on Karlovo namesti that the city later attaches to the legend. The line running back from Dee's angel conversations to a Benedictine abbot's manual of angel-writing is a line of reading, not of acquaintance. Trithemius has been dead eighty-four years and his most notorious book is still not in print.
sources: johann_faust.journey.json (stop 'Prague, the Faust House on Karlovo namesti', citing the Trithemius-Dee-Fludd thread from QUEUE.md)
QUEUE.md line 254 (John Dee entry, pre-linked to Trithemius)
suggested_refs: John Dee and Robert Fludd, both queued and not yet researched, whose files will inherit this thread

stops.name: Heidelberg, the library arrives where the boy studied
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year for the library transfer and for Freher's edition; no source connects the two events
stops.campa: The Sponheim collection, dispersed after the abbey closed in 1556, reaches Heidelberg and is folded into the Bibliotheca Palatina, in the town where a runaway of seventeen studied for three years before a snowstorm turned him into a monk. In the same year the jurist Marquard Freher publishes the first collected edition of his works, and Johannes Busaeus follows between 1604 and 1624. In 1622 the Palatina is packed onto mules and carried over the Alps to Rome.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Kloster Sponheim' (library to Heidelberg 1601, to Rome 1622-23)
suggested_refs: The Bibliotheca Palatina, into which the Sponheim books were absorbed before their removal to the Vatican

stops.name: Frankfurt, Steganographia in print with its key
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: A hundred and six years after it was written, the book of angel magic is finally printed at Frankfurt, and printed together with a key. The key shows what the first two books actually are: the invocations are cover, the angel names are cipher, and the entire apparatus of spirits is a delivery system for hidden text. The third book is left standing as genuine occultism, because nobody in 1606 can crack it. It will hold out another three hundred and ninety years.
suggested_refs: The 1606 Frankfurt edition of Steganographia, printed with the Clavis that decodes Books I and II

stops.name: Rome, the Index
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: Three years after it is printed with the key that explains it, Steganographia is placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum. The demonstration that the book is cryptography rather than conjuration does not save it; the reputation built in manuscript is by now older and louder than the evidence against it. Nine years earlier, in the Campo de' Fiori a few streets from here, Giordano Bruno was burned for heresies the age filed under magic. Trithemius, who wrote out more angel names than Bruno ever did, died an abbot in his own bed.
sources: johann_faust.journey.json (stop, Rome, citing the Bruno file)
suggested_refs: The Index Librorum Prohibitorum entry for Steganographia, 1609-1900

stops.name: Munich, the bust in the Ruhmeshalle
stops.date_confidence: the hall opened in 1853 and the bust itself is undated in the source; the hall was war-damaged and reopened on 26 October 1972
stops.campa: Bavaria builds a colonnade above the Theresienhöhe to hold the busts of its worthies, and Trithemius is set into the left-hand wall with two words cut under him: ABT U. GELEHRTER, abbot and scholar. Neither word is cryptographer, magician, or forger. The state that chose him chose the least contested version of the man, three hundred and thirty-seven years after his death, and the marble says nothing about Faust. The hall is wrecked in the war and reopens in October 1972 with the busts back in their niches.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Ruhmeshalle (München)' (left side wall, inscribed ABT U. GELEHRTER)
suggested_refs: The Ruhmeshalle on the Theresienhöhe, Munich, where the bust stands on the left side wall

stops.name: Rome, struck from the Index
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year
stops.campa: After two hundred and ninety-one years Steganographia comes off the list of prohibited books. By 1900 the ciphers of its first two books have been public for nearly three centuries, and the tabula recta of Polygraphia is a schoolroom exercise in every European army's signals office. The prohibition outlasts by nearly three centuries the secrecy it was meant to enforce. Nobody records who asked for the removal, or why the case was reopened in that particular year.
sources: English Wikipedia, 'Steganographia' (removed from the Index in 1900)
suggested_refs: The 1900 revision of the Index, which released Steganographia after 291 years

stops.name: Trittenheim, the village puts up a statue
stops.date_confidence: the year 1962 is attested by German Wikipedia; the statue's position in the village is not recorded anywhere reachable, and the pin sits at the village centre
stops.campa: Five hundred years after the birth, the wine village on the Moselle raises a standing figure of Johannes Trithemius among its sights. The boy who was forbidden his books here by a stepfather, and who left at seventeen and never lived here again, comes back as the thing the place is known for besides its Riesling. No source says where in the village the statue stands, so the pin sits at the centre of it. The German article lists the standing figure among the village sights and gives it no site.
sources: German Wikipedia, 'Trittenheim' (Standbild listed among the village sights, undated)
suggested_refs: The 1962 Standbild of Johannes Trithemius at Trittenheim, whose exact site is unrecorded

stops.name: Sponheim, the third book gives way
stops.date_confidence: Thomas Ernst published the solution in Daphnis in 1996; Jim Reeds published an independent solution in Cryptologia in 1998, and the two are routinely collapsed into one event
stops.campa: Four hundred and ninety-six years after it was written, the third book of Steganographia is read. Thomas Ernst shows in 1996 that its remaining angel magic is itself enciphered text, and Jim Reeds, working independently, publishes the same result in 1998. Nothing in the book was ever what it said it was. The pin sits on the ruin where it was written, because a decipherment happens in journals and has no geography of its own, and because this is the room the sentences were composed in.
sources: Thomas Ernst, 'Schwarzweisse Magie: Der Schlüssel zum dritten Buch der Steganographia des Trithemius', Daphnis, 1996
Jim Reeds, 'Solved: The Ciphers in Book III of Trithemius's Steganographia', Cryptologia, 1998
suggested_refs: Ernst 1996 and Reeds 1998, two independent solutions of Book III, habitually cited as one
